title: Social Exclusion in the Arts: The Dynamics of Social and Economic Mobility Across Three Decades of Undergraduate Arts Alumni in the United States
text_snippet: Social Exclusion in the Arts: The Dynamics of Social and Economic Mobility Across Three Decades of Undergraduate Arts Alumni in the United States This chapter presents a broad interdisciplinary literature review linking artists’ economic precarity and need for but resistance to entrepreneurial skills, alongside colonial histories, structural racism, and hierarchies of taste in arts organizations. These themes are complemented empirically by engaging data from the Strategic National Arts Alumni Project (SNAAP) to demonstrate indicators of attrition and privilege of arts alumni relative to their participation in the arts workforce. Meaningfully different associations across racial/ethnic groups are uncovered, showing structural exclusion of Black arts alumni in particular, in addition to other intersectional dynamics. This chapter underscores the importance of addressing student debt, the potential of creative pedagogies across the curriculum, and the need for imaginative approaches to renewed public funding of art and artists.

title: Black Brilliance and Creative Problem Solving in Fugitive Spaces: Advancing the BlackCreate Framework Through a Systematic Review
text_snippet: Black Brilliance and Creative Problem Solving in Fugitive Spaces: Advancing the BlackCreate Framework Through a Systematic Review Traditional definitions and assessments of creativity often neglect to identify the complexity surrounding Black students’ brilliance, leading to lack of access and funding. Further, even when recognized, Black students are often funneled into programs that do not facilitate positive development of their racial-ethnic identity. Through our systematic review of 155 publications, we developed the BlackCreate Framework to illustrate how effective Black creative educational experiences (BCEEs) create fugitive spaces for creative expression and education. Within these spaces, both societal oppression and community assets are explicitly discussed as a part of the creative process, providing students methods for adaptive coping and for addressing systemic inequities. Given these findings, we advocate for consistent funding and support for fugitive spaces to promote Black students’ creativity.

title: Democratizing Creative Educational Experiences
text_snippet: Democratizing Creative Educational Experiences

title: To Democratize, First Decolonize: Approaches Beyond Eurocentric and Colonial Epistemologies in Creativity
text_snippet: To Democratize, First Decolonize: Approaches Beyond Eurocentric and Colonial Epistemologies in Creativity In response to the special issue on democratizing creative educational experiences (CEE), we conducted a thematic analysis of recent scholarship on creativity and decolonization (2010–2021) and analyzed recurring tensions across literature grounded in Indigenous, Black, feminist, and non-western epistemological perspectives on creativity. We found themes that are not new but are yet to be taken up consistently and credibly in western creativity and education research and practice. For instance, spirituality emerges as a valuable ingredient for creativity, body as inseparable from the mind, dialectic resistance and resilience as acts of creative existence, and non-human agency as essential to the creative process. Informed by these themes, we share implications for research and practice, seeking new spaces inclusive of historically ignored onto-epistemologies.

title: Transdisciplinarity: Re-Visioning How Sciences and Arts Together Can Enact Democratizing Creative Educational Experiences
text_snippet: Transdisciplinarity: Re-Visioning How Sciences and Arts Together Can Enact Democratizing Creative Educational Experiences The movement from STEM to STEAM, with its emphasis on real-world applications, promises to meet the changing needs of a globally connected world. However, the potential of transdisciplinarity to inspire and deepen our understanding of who we are and how we make sense of a world in turmoil remains undertheorized. This article makes a case for repositioning STEAM education as democratized enactments of transdisciplinary education, where arts and sciences are not separate or even separable endeavors. Drawing upon posthumanist theorizing, three projects will exemplify transdisciplinarity across music, mathematics, and science education. Transgressing and transcending disciplinary boundaries, and attending to both human and nonhuman perspectives, we invite a rethink of the work of schools, going beyond democratizing creativity to fully enact posthumanist transdisciplinarity.

title: Creativity as a Racializing and Ableizing Scientific Object: Disentangling the Democratic Impulse From Justice-Oriented Futures
text_snippet: Creativity as a Racializing and Ableizing Scientific Object: Disentangling the Democratic Impulse From Justice-Oriented Futures In this review of literature, we attend to some of the ways that well-intentioned hopes for fostering creativity and encouraging greater inclusion may also rely on problematic premises that work to reify exclusionary logics and practices. More specifically, we historicize and critically examine how creativity studies—often despite explicit efforts to broaden notions of creativity, include marginalized populations, and democratize education—have differently reanimated racializing and ableizing discourses over seven decades of efforts to scientifically study, define, and/or cultivate creativity. In our emphasis on the relationship between past and present designs, we attend to more pernicious tensions and concerns that continue to hold implications for scholarship, research, policy, and practice.

title: Posthuman Creativities: Democratizing Creative Educational Experience Beyond the Human
text_snippet: Posthuman Creativities: Democratizing Creative Educational Experience Beyond the Human This chapter explores the urgent relevance of posthumanist theory and practice for democratizing creative educational experiences in 21st-century schools, universities, and informal learning environments. Posthumanism challenges the myopic centering of the human in creative education in an age of climate change, artificial intelligence, and zoonotic disease, where nonhuman agencies are intricately imbricated in human cultures and lives. Using a cartographic methodology, the chapter critically maps key theories and debates in posthumanist creativity studies across four substantive fields of inquiry: (a) process philosophy, (b) affect studies, (c) place-based education, and (d) creative ecology. Drawing links between theoretical concepts and practical examples of creative experience across formal and informal education contexts, the chapter scopes an alternative agenda for critical studies of creativity in light of the posthuman turn.

title: Creative Methods for Creativity Research(ers)? Speculations
text_snippet: Creative Methods for Creativity Research(ers)? Speculations Creativity forms a part of educational curriculum and is an important element of education research. Clearly, creativity research of the past has made a great impact in the ways in which creativity has been integrated within education and educational practice. Yet how creativity has been studied and how the methodologies of these studies shape produced knowledge and impact educational practice are still rather limited and limiting. This chapter calls for methodological experimentation, various forms of performativity, and creativity in the context of research utilizing speculative wonderings. We situate our arguments in different trends in creativity research and discuss more methodologically diverse, speculative, and creative futures.

title: Connected Arts Learning: Cultivating Equity Through Connected and Creative Educational Experiences
text_snippet: Connected Arts Learning: Cultivating Equity Through Connected and Creative Educational Experiences This review brings together scholarship from creative educational experiences (CEE) and connected learning to describe a connected arts learning framework, reframing arts education in the 21st century with a focus on connecting youths’ interest-driven art making to opportunities through supportive relationships. Such a framework pushes the arts education field to consider outcomes beyond artistic skill acquisition and academic achievement to include a broader range of opportunities, including those civic- and career-related; promote interest development through targeted exposure to new forms of art making; create and implement professional development and programming to emphasize networks and connections; and draw from culturally sustaining practices to bridge connections between spaces for learning. A connected learning lens applied to what we know about high quality arts education sharpens our focus on how CEE can cultivate equity and social/cultural connection for youth.

title: Unapologetically Black Creative Educational Experiences in Higher Education: A Critical Review
text_snippet: Unapologetically Black Creative Educational Experiences in Higher Education: A Critical Review Black creative educational experiences (BCEEs) are participatory, performative cultural experiences created by or for students, centering Black artistic expression, aesthetics, and engagement. Using African-centered frameworks, we provide a methodological guide for examining BCEEs in education research, which includes centering Black “ways of knowing,” validating creative expressions cultivated by and for Black people, acknowledging the influence of Black creative expression on research and practice, considering researcher positionalities as observers and cultivators of Black creative expression, and viewing Black creative expression as knowledge production. We found BCEEs are democratizing educational experiences rooted in intellectual and expressive freedom (freedom of movement/voice/tongue), and community building. BCEEs should be centered in education research, particularly postsecondary education, and prioritized in institutional programming, curricula, and high-impact practices.

title: Democratizing Creative Early Educational Experiences: A Matter of Racial Justice
text_snippet: Democratizing Creative Early Educational Experiences: A Matter of Racial Justice Inquiring into the democratization of creative early educational experiences through the lens of the politics of belonging, this review of research asks: What does research reveal about creative early educational experiences as they pertain to history, race, and justice? Seeking to better understand the racialization of creative early educational experiences, this review undertakes a transformative justice in education approach, attending to the historical roots of the contemporary racialized politics of belonging. Despite the creativity, improvisation, and imagination displayed historically by Black, Indigenous, and other Communities of Color, findings underscore how creative educational experiences prioritize Eurocentric onto-epistemologies, (re)inscribing inequitable schooling. Creative disruption and Black futurities offer two possible pathways to disrupt the legacy of racism in U.S. early schooling.

title: Exploring Conceptions of Creativity and Latinidad in Environmental Education Through the Lens of Culturally Sustaining Pedagogy
text_snippet: Exploring Conceptions of Creativity and Latinidad in Environmental Education Through the Lens of Culturally Sustaining Pedagogy Environmental education seeks to foster meaningful connections to local and global environments through creative nature experiences. Responding to critiques of historical inequities, practitioners are prioritizing equitable access for historically marginalized youth, particularly from Black, Indigenous, and Latinx communities; this identity-centered prioritization, while essential, generates questions of normativity, diversity, relevance, and engagement within identity groups. Drawing on creativity as meaningful person-world encounters characterized by pluriperspective, future-oriented, nonlinear, and open-ended qualities, this chapter uses culturally sustaining pedagogy to explore how environmental education studies (a) operationalize Latinidad and associated constructs, (b) enact creative experiences in environmental education, and (c) qualify the roles of Latinx communities in shaping these creative experiences. We review studies of environmental education with Latinx youth in the United States that explicitly employ culturally sustaining approaches to engage these communities. We bring together these frameworks as a strategy to move beyond discrete notions of Latinidad in envir

title: A Critical Review of Assessments of Creativity in Education
text_snippet: A Critical Review of Assessments of Creativity in Education This chapter provides a systematic, synthesizing, and critical review of the literature related to assessments of creativity in education from historical, theoretical, empirical, and practical standpoints. We examined the assessments used in the articles focusing on education that are published from January 2010 to May 2021 in eight creativity, psychological, and educational journals. We found that the assessments of creativity in education are split between psychological and education research and have increased international participation. Additionally, these assessments are more general than specific and focus more on cognitive than noncognitive aspects. Like previous reviews of assessments of creativity in general, this review showed that creativity in education is still mainly assessed by divergent thinking or creativity tests, self-report questionnaires, and product-based subjective techniques. We analyzed the benefits and drawbacks of each approach and highlighted many innovations in the assessment. We further discussed how the major assessment approaches address race, ethnicity, class, and gender issues in education. We concluded the review with recommendations for how to b

title: Strong Starts, Just Futures: Health, Socioeconomic Stability, and Children’s Rights in Early Learning
text_snippet: Strong Starts, Just Futures: Health, Socioeconomic Stability, and Children’s Rights in Early Learning For decades, research has shown what children need to grow up healthy and well, reiterating what families have always known: Children need consistent, warm, and responsive caregivers. Children also need access to quality, unbiased health care; socioeconomic security that can facilitate stable housing, nutritious food, and well-resourced, safe communities; and quality education, particularly early education. These critical areas of well-being are interrelated and intertwined in their impact on children’s development and learning. And the conditions to nurture each area are not—nor have ever been—evenly or fairly accessible across sociodemographic groups. This chapter focuses on these issues and the urgency to create educational and social contexts that can promote just futures for young children, especially those from historically marginalized communities

title: Maybe All That’s Left Is Hard Work: Abolition, Black Feminism, Emergent Strategy, and Freedom Dreaming for Thriving
text_snippet: Maybe All That’s Left Is Hard Work: Abolition, Black Feminism, Emergent Strategy, and Freedom Dreaming for Thriving There is no single way to cultivate thriving, especially when pursuing equity-focused approaches for large-scale systems change. This chapter examines the predictable failures of equity reform, showing how such efforts are often undermined by “toxic supremacies.” The work is complex and difficult to sustain, shaped by histories of harm that extend far beyond the current generation of students. Still, we must try again and again, becoming more human each time. I argue that our road map must be grounded in abolition, Black feminism, emergent strategy, and freedom dreaming—frameworks that invite us to imagine beyond harm and build toward possibility. Thriving emerges through communal care, joy, repair, and accountability—the hard work that remains.

title: Collectively Imagining and Designing for Transformative Futures Through Rightful Familial Engagement in STEM Education
text_snippet: Collectively Imagining and Designing for Transformative Futures Through Rightful Familial Engagement in STEM Education Systems of schooling and STEM have been organized around White supremacy and middle-class values and practices that sideline minoritized students and families. Although White middle-class families exert significant influence on their children’s schooling and by extension, other children, families of minoritized students typically have experienced fewer such opportunities. We take up family engagement in STEM education as a contested equity terrain with attention to minoritized families and communities. Our critical metasynthesis points to the need for systems transformation vis-à-vis familial rightful presence, a logic that emphasizes new ethical relations that redefine the social institutions and contours of engagement. The four underpinning principles of this logic collectively create the conditions for new, thriving futures for families and schools that are just and healthy. They include (a) spatial and temporal resonances, (b) solidarity toward equitable collaboration and coordination for the here and now and toward desired futures, (c) collective responsibility for family-engaged justice-oriented STEM, and (d) STEM for thriving, recognition, and critical democratic citizenry.

title: Bridging Research, Policy, and Practice: A Systematic Review of Climate Change Education Across Fields Through a Justice Lens (2014–2024)
text_snippet: Bridging Research, Policy, and Practice: A Systematic Review of Climate Change Education Across Fields Through a Justice Lens (2014–2024) This systematic review synthesizes a decade of climate change education research (2014–2024) across 24 high-impact journals in general education, science/STEM, and environmental/geography education. Using a justice-oriented analytic framework grounded in community and equity, rooted in place and relations, and oriented toward action and transformation, we analyzed 257 empirical studies to identify trends, gaps, and exemplars. Findings reveal uneven yet significant progress: Justice-centered approaches are most prevalent in environmental and geography education (≈52%), emerging in science/STEM (≈17%), and comparatively limited in general education (≈21%). Across fields, scholarship has shifted from cognitive and individualistic models toward participatory, relational, and community-based approaches that connect learning to civic and ecological action. Two illustrative cases, Learning in Places and an anticolonial, community-driven pedagogy in Eswatini, demonstrate how intergenerational, place-based, and care-centered infrastructures advance justice in practice. We conclude by calling for stronger cross-disciplinary collaboration, greater representation in high-impact education journ

title: Embracing Tensions: Professional Formation in the Age of Complexity
text_snippet: Embracing Tensions: Professional Formation in the Age of Complexity This commentary frames tension as foundational within education systems at the nexus of scholar preparation. This volume’s call underscores tension as an undeniable aspect of ensuring complex systems for collective well-being. Sometimes, tensions appear as tussles between right and wrong. More often, tensions appear between multiple legitimate rights. Whether a tension presents itself as right versus wrong or right versus right, helpful education researchers must recognize tensions for what they are and understand how to work within them. Navigating the challenges of legitimate rights is a fundamental preparation challenge that today’s infrastructure in graduate schools and other venues must meet if the next generation of scholars is to be effective helpers and improvers in complex educational ecologies.

title: Studying Relation and Return: Axioms for the Field of Education Research
text_snippet: Studying Relation and Return: Axioms for the Field of Education Research As an interdisciplinary field grown from other intellectual traditions, education research can have an undefined disciplinarity. The author argues that the field of education research has inherited an ineffectiveness in addressing roots of inequality, in part because the roots are dismissed as too old, too tangled, too deep, and too expansive to possibly address. This chapter defines a core set of commitments, not to convey settled agreement but to spark conversation about the ethical and epistemological imperatives that are specific to the field of education research. The axioms offered are indeed provocative, meant to inspire conversation in the field about the commitments and aims of education research and its future trajectories.

title: Excavating Axiological Positivity From Deaf Education Research: A Critical Scoping Review
text_snippet: Excavating Axiological Positivity From Deaf Education Research: A Critical Scoping Review Contemporary deaf education is adopting increasingly prosocial teaching methods and asset-based research methodologies; however, major disparities persist. As paradigms shift, a paradox emerges: Promising future developments clash with historical injustices. Therefore, we conducted a critical and generative scoping review intended to excavate an evidentiary conceptual framework, which we call “axiological positivity in deaf education.” We identified 32 studies representing 10 years (2014–2024) of deaf education research leveraging prosocial teaching frameworks and asset-based research methodologies. Our review is interpreted through a critical deaf pedagogy research lens. We report five focused themes and three categories of findings about beneficent, harm-reducing approaches in deaf education. We also present four asset-based methodological discussions to guide future research. Overall, we advocate an optimistic, wholesome outlook for deaf education as it transforms. We believe that by situating our research rationale and then synthesizing high-quality empirical evidence, axiological positivity can allow deaf education to flourish in our time.

title: Ontological Realities and Futures: Collectivity and New Imaginings
text_snippet: Ontological Realities and Futures: Collectivity and New Imaginings This chapter calls for the field of education to find ways to move together in facing an uncertain future. It asks: How might we imagine deep connections between equity, building and strengthening capacity, and futures on a planet whose environment, technology, and societal structures are changing faster than ever? And how do we imagine a future when this change may never again be this slow? How do we, as a field, plan for a future of work and scholarship that is opaque? I argue that “equity” is a verb—something we do—and is part of our work with and for children and the future. I call for collectivity, a clear sense of purpose, a commitment to supporting children, and a commitment to agreeing and disagreeing toward the ends of doing right rather than being right.

title: On Building a Local SEL Ecosystem to Advance Thriving, Equity and Excellence
text_snippet: On Building a Local SEL Ecosystem to Advance Thriving, Equity and Excellence This chapter briefly describes key aspects of my and my coauthors’ work on transformative social emotional learning (tSEL). First, we provide background framing for tSEL and its connections to civic engagement and thriving. Following this, we offer a description of the focal constructs of identity, agency, belonging, collaborative problem-solving, and curiosity as relevant instantiations of the five most prevalent social emotional learning core competence domains (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making). Lastly, we highlight the utility of inquiry-based practices, especially community-based participatory action research, for co-constructing local learning ecosystems that might support the development of tSEL competencies and related developmental outcomes while contributing to individual and collective thriving for participating and affected young people and adults.

title: An Equity Agenda at Work: A Citation Context Analysis of Connected Learning Research
text_snippet: An Equity Agenda at Work: A Citation Context Analysis of Connected Learning Research This integrative review analyzes the uptake of Connected Learning: An Agenda for Research and Design (referred to hereafter as “the Agenda”), which advocated for a radical rethinking of education that honors youths’ lifewide learning across networked technologies. This white paper introduced a robust equity agenda to ensure young people, particularly multiply marginalized youth and their communities, thrive across spheres of their lives. Using citation context analysis, we examined 554 juried manuscripts published between 2013 and 2019 that cited the Agenda, drawn from an initial corpus of 871 works across diverse disciplines and global contexts. The review highlights promising expansions of the Agenda’s theory of change, including conceptualizations that shifted from context-bound views of learning to fluid, equity-oriented ecologies; treatments of “interest” as relational, historically situated, dynamic, and infrastructurally supported; and positionings of adults as agentive brokers and sponsors facilitating the navigation and intervention of inequitable learning ecologies. We also surface persistent tensions, highlighting that while 27.8% of manuscripts engaged connected learnin

title: Reflections on Equity-Focused Policy Research
text_snippet: Reflections on Equity-Focused Policy Research Quantitative research on educational equity is being reshaped by rapid expansion in data sources, analytic tools, and research partnerships. In this chapter, I consider how emerging forms of data are influencing the questions researchers pose and expanding the scope of educational inquiry while also showing how partnerships create opportunities for more policy-relevant analyses that support systemic reform. Drawing on my experiences as an equity-focused policy scholar, I argue that advancing equity requires deeper researcher engagement in data acquisition, stronger understanding of educational systems and practitioners’ decision-making needs, and a commitment to methodological flexibility and reflexivity.

title: Reimagining Sanctuary in the Context of U.S. Immigration Policy: Five Expanded Dimensions to Support Immigrant Children and Families
text_snippet: Reimagining Sanctuary in the Context of U.S. Immigration Policy: Five Expanded Dimensions to Support Immigrant Children and Families The thriving of immigrant children and families is currently under severe threat in the United States. This population, particularly those with liminal legal status but also much more broadly, has been singled out for policy attacks that threaten the historic roots of thriving for immigrants in the United States—access, integration, inclusion, and belonging in educational and other systems. We propose that to provide the context and resources necessary to support the thriving of immigrant children and families in the current policy climate, we must consider the notion of sanctuary. We present an expanded conceptualization of sanctuary that encompasses social, physical/geographic, political, legal, and narrative dimensions and may inform a long-term vision for immigration and education policy.

title: 50 Years of Multilingual Education Research: Transforming Toward Multilingual Community Thriving
text_snippet: 50 Years of Multilingual Education Research: Transforming Toward Multilingual Community Thriving This review grapples with 50 years of historical and contemporary tensions related to equity conceived, measured, and imagined in pre-K–12 settings for multilingual students through a research as intersectional racialized social practice lens. Starting with 632 studies that met our inclusion criteria, we analyzed research problems and questions, theoretical frameworks, methodologies, and patterns in findings and implications to identify 464 studies that attended to multilingualism beyond naming it as a student demographic variable. These studies were then sorted according to their conceptualizations of equity—as access to a dominant variety of English, as access to bilingualism, and/or as transformation (informed by Grapin). The studies that conceptualized equity as transformation were analyzed in depth for their methodological and pedagogical practices and impacts, offering transformative praxis possibilities to support multilingual community thriving. This review serves as an invitation to multilingual education researchers to center racially just multilingualism, thoughtfully operationalize equity in terms of transformation, and engage in research that disrupts monolithic notion

title: Toward a Framework of Jotería Thriving in Education: Rethinking Research Paradigms on Queer/Trans Latinx Learning
text_snippet: Toward a Framework of Jotería Thriving in Education: Rethinking Research Paradigms on Queer/Trans Latinx Learning This chapter reframes research on queer and trans (QT) Latinx learning by shifting the focus from documenting harm to designing livable educational worlds. Drawing on a multilingual, Américas-wide systematic review (N = 112) and decolonial, feminist, and queer-of-color traditions, we propose jotería thriving as a paradigm for research, policy, and practice. This paradigm organizes seven mutually reinforcing design levers across K–12, higher education (especially Hispanic-serving institutions), and informal learning. We follow scholars who critique damage-centered, race-neutral “LGBTQ” framings and positivist logics that individualize risk and mask structure. Our methodological approach includes queer pláticas/testimonio, design- and arts-based inquiry, and critical quantitative traditions (QuantCrit, QuantQueer). Survivor-safe ethics are paired with actionable indicators of belonging, safety, kinship density, spatial access, leadership, and joy/futurity as well as decolonial measures that explicitly name the colonial gender continuum, colonial dysphoria, and institutional trans violence. Together, these measures anchor institutional accountability. We offer a practice-oriented fram

title: Systematic Review of Cross-National Research on Building Equitable Education Systems: Exploring Perspectives and Approaches
text_snippet: Systematic Review of Cross-National Research on Building Equitable Education Systems: Exploring Perspectives and Approaches Reform discourses globally are increasingly focused on education system transformation for equity. However, there is a relatively small research base explicitly addressing this topic. In this chapter, we conduct a systematic review of international research literature (N = 52 publications) at the intersection of systems transformation/change and equity to uncover what inequities motivate researchers’ work, how equity is conceptualized across international contexts, and what examples exist of systems that have transformed for equitable education. We find “equity,” “systems,” and “transformation” are contested and complex terms situated in historical and sociopolitical contexts. Rather than reinvention, transformation as evolution was a more prevalent approach. The framing of problems and conceptualizations of equity have consequences for the work of system transformation, and thus, more nuanced theorizing and conceptualization about what constitutes the system, equity, and transformation are needed. The findings raise questions for thinking about educational transformation for equity in research and practice.

title: SHIFTing Social and Emotional Learning for Equity: A Systemic and Humanizing Implementation Focused on Transformation
text_snippet: SHIFTing Social and Emotional Learning for Equity: A Systemic and Humanizing Implementation Focused on Transformation Social and emotional learning (SEL) has historically been driven by the pursuit of improved individual-level outcomes—with sparse guidance for systemic implementation and insufficient attention to systemic inequities. We provide the first synthesis of how macrosystems and equity are discussed in the published literature about SEL implementation, and what their invocation lends to a reimagined practice toward equitable thriving in schools. This article first inspires and then conducts a systematic search of four bodies of literature (systemic SEL, transformative SEL, implementation science in SEL, and humanizing alternatives to SEL) in hopes of weaving together their strengths and overcoming their respective vulnerabilities for shifting practice. We provide a scoping review of 116 publications, identifying motivations, conceptualizations, contradictions, and innovations for equity in and through SEL. Although we do not resolve the exposed tensions, we organize them within a productive synthesis of 10 ecological assets for improving the conditions for equitable thriving in schools. Based on this review, we reconceptualize equitable thriving to hold individual thriving in dynamic rela

title: Defining Social Justice Leadership in Education: A Critical Systematic Review
text_snippet: Defining Social Justice Leadership in Education: A Critical Systematic Review Over the last 2 decades, social justice leadership (SJL) has been a prominent topic, yet a consensus definition that effectively explains the concept and its scope remains elusive. This study critically reviews 62 peer-reviewed articles to analyze how scholars have defined SJL in educational settings and identify a meaningful, adaptable consensus definition that serves research- and practice-oriented needs in education. This consensus definition addresses several long-standing challenges and tensions in the scholarship. First, this definition overcomes the ambiguous nature of SJL scholarship that can allow well-intended leadership efforts to inadvertently maintain deficit perspectives. Second, this definition frames SJL as an ecological and systemic process rather than individualistic and hierarchical. Third, this definition captures international and PK–16 educational perspectives, overcoming the siloing tendency of SJL research. By clarifying a consensus definition of SJL and addressing these tensions, this study offers a guiding framework of SJL for current and aspiring educational leaders and scholars who are committed to advancing educational systems that cultivate collective

title: Immigration Enforcement as Community Violence: Understanding the Implications of Attacks on Immigrant Families for Schools and Transforming Education Systems to Respond
text_snippet: Immigration Enforcement as Community Violence: Understanding the Implications of Attacks on Immigrant Families for Schools and Transforming Education Systems to Respond In this chapter, we offer our vision for educational transformation in which schools promote thriving for immigrant-origin youth. Drawing on research about the consequences of immigration enforcement for young people, the powerful role of educators in immigrant-origin students’ lives, and the knowledge that educators need to build strong relationships with immigrant-origin students, we engage with two of the main tensions that have challenged scholarship on equity and justice. First, we highlight the ways that anti-immigrant policies, rhetoric, and actions function as a collective problem and not one reserved to those individuals most vulnerable to deportation. We also focus on transforming teacher preparation, in-service training, and professional development as a part of the larger set of systemic reforms necessary for educational institutions to fulfill their mission and obligation to immigrant-origin students and families.

title: Advancing an Equitable and Just Early Care and Education Ecosystem Through Community-Based Research Partnerships
text_snippet: Advancing an Equitable and Just Early Care and Education Ecosystem Through Community-Based Research Partnerships Scholars, policymakers, and practitioners have spent decades engaging in efforts to expand access to high-quality early learning experiences for children from birth to age 5. Expressed as benevolent acts to support children and families, these efforts are also grounded in capitalist aims to expand the workforce and settler colonial constructs of assimilation. In this chapter, we unpack equity in early learning, guided by the current evidence on community-based research partnerships (CBRPs) and focused on equity with respect to access, experiences, and positive outcomes. Such partnerships can promote efforts to actively and continuously identify and eliminate manifestations of systemic racism and other forms of oppression throughout the research-to-action enterprise. We reflect the broad and emerging areas that represent the potential of CBRPs from three examples working to enact equitable systems toward just, sustainable futures. Lastly, we draw on the R.I.C.H.E.R., a framework focused on reeducation about the history of oppression, integration of lived experiences and extant evidence, critical consciousness about structural inequities, having humility of privilege, erasing racism

title: Racial Equity in School Funding Policies and Processes: A Scoping Review
text_snippet: Racial Equity in School Funding Policies and Processes: A Scoping Review Research on racial equity in school finance is spread across several thought traditions. However, it was unclear which traditions have contributed to our understanding of possible solutions to inequitable funding and which ones may be underrepresented. In this scoping review, I synthesize 54 articles and find that this research exists across three primary areas: education law, economics of education, and critical analysis. Across these three areas, racial equity is conceptualized differently, which leads to different racial equity goals and desired outcomes across paradigms. These differences generate tensions as scholars and practitioners work toward multisystemic solutions. I uplift interdisciplinarity as a strategic way forward, suggesting that researchers lean into these tensions to establish effective long-term funding solutions that support student thriving.

title: From Problem to Possibility: A Systematic Review of Teacher Education Research on Social Justice, 2012–2021
text_snippet: From Problem to Possibility: A Systematic Review of Teacher Education Research on Social Justice, 2012–2021 This study systematically reviews teacher education research on social justice from 2012 to 2021, examining patterns in how scholars make the justice claims that motivate their work. Through a systematic search, we identify a corpus of 1,466 articles and analyze a random sample of 255 articles using codes derived from theories of justice. We find that the vast majority of scholarship has relied on three distinct frames of social justice: (a) injustice as the inequitable distribution of resources, (b) injustice as material inequity, and (c) injustice as unquestioned dominant norms. The most significant finding of our analysis is the stubborn absence, across nearly all of the literature, of justice claims employing a rare fourth frame of justice as a possibility rather than injustice as a problem. We call for an expansion of possibility rather than problem frames in education research, arguing that such a shift may support the field in constructing liberatory educational futures that stretch beyond the constraints of the traditional social science genre.

title: A Model of Latinx Racialization: Multiple Dimensions and (Mis)Alignments in Educational Equity
text_snippet: A Model of Latinx Racialization: Multiple Dimensions and (Mis)Alignments in Educational Equity Latinx educational outcomes have improved in recent years, yet acute racialized inequities persist and complicate even well-intentioned equity efforts. Drawing on Vargas, Valle, and Dhuman’s (2025) multidimensional model of racialization (hereafter, the VVD model), we argue that understanding and addressing Latinx educational inequities requires grappling with a core dual challenge: Equity work must account for mechanisms of aggregate-level Latinx racialization that produce between-group inequities in relation to other broadly racialized populations, while simultaneously attending to mechanisms of racialized inequity within the Latinx population. Addressing inequities also requires grappling with what we refer to as racialized (mis)alignments between three dimensions of racialization (identification, ascription, and structural racism). We demonstrate the utility of the VVD model by examining racialization pertaining to immigration, colorism, and Afro-Latinx and Indigenous Latinx students’ experiences. Finally, we offer a practitioner-facing use-case exemplar of the VVD model and encourage its adaptation for other racialized populations.

title: Who Cares? Practices of Livingness Amid the Educational Rubble
text_snippet: Who Cares? Practices of Livingness Amid the Educational Rubble From do-it-yourself/ves practices to meal trains, consciousness-raising groups, and various forms of creative worldmaking, care has been a central animating concept to subaltern livingness. In this chapter, we attune toward care as an endarkened, disabled, and queer concept. That is, we seek to remember, recover, and envision resistant practices of how care has continually been crafted as a way to support and promote livingness for those most on the margins. In doing so, we create an archive of livingness, or a process calling forth those “literatures” that although perhaps not in the “academic record” are invaluable in detailing potentialities otherwise under the ongoing conditions of institutional—which is to say, educational—control. We put these networks, sites, and knowings into conversation with/through each other to embody deeper and messier care and relationality. Stemming from two questions (What does care make you do? What does care make you be?), we encourage readers to imagine practices for thriving and creating, including those extending beyond and/or already occurring outside of institutionally recognized channels.

title: Between Man and AI: Human-Centered Design and the Promise for Educational Equity
text_snippet: Between Man and AI: Human-Centered Design and the Promise for Educational Equity This chapter critically examines the assumptions underlying human-centered design (HCD) and human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) as frameworks for achieving equity in education. It is argued that these approaches reproduce the Enlightenment category of “the Human,” whose overrepresentation sustains racial, colonial, and economic hierarchies. Drawing on Sylvia Wynter and related cultural theorists, it is delineated how HCD/HCAI’s claims to fairness depend on a normative, universal human subject that fixes difference as deficit and limits transformative potential. We proffer a proposal that gestures toward an alternative praxis to HCD and HCAI. Drawing on our own experimentations with this methodology, our approach disavows placing “the Human” at the center and instead engages AI through relational, decolonial, and plural epistemologies to advance truly equitable educational futures.

title: Tracing the Roots of Black Education Studies: A Tale of Four Scholars
text_snippet: Tracing the Roots of Black Education Studies: A Tale of Four Scholars This essay charts the relationship between Black studies and education research by attending to key intellectual contributions by four scholars: Jane Ellen McAllister, the first African American woman to earn a doctorate in education; James D. Anderson, a scholar of Black educational history; June Jordan, an architect of Black studies; and Joyce King, a scholar who developed a Black studies approach to education research. Engaging their contributions, we highlight a symbiotic relationship between Black studies and African American intellectual thought in education, a relationship that informs a field of research recently named “Black education studies.” After reviewing this scholarly tradition, we discuss how it might be garnered in the contemporary moment to support the development of emerging scholars and research.

title: Advancing Theory, Method, and Praxis to Confront Racial Stress and Trauma in Schools
text_snippet: Advancing Theory, Method, and Praxis to Confront Racial Stress and Trauma in Schools Despite growing recognition of trauma in schools, most trauma-informed frameworks overlook racism as a systemic and chronic source of harm, focusing instead on individual symptoms detached from historical harm and structural conditions. Advancing equity requires theory, methods, and praxis that illuminate how racial stress and trauma (RST) operate across the school ecology—from policies to adults to youth—and how collective healing is possible. This commentary calls for healing-centered, racially conscious approaches that confront structural inequities while cultivating agency, belonging, and hope. We outline the problem of RST in current sociopolitical context and offer recommendations to expand theory, diversify methods, and reimagine school-based praxis to disrupt racial harm and promote justice, well-being, and thriving. We call for interdisciplinary collaboration centering healing and equity.

title: Language Thriving: Insights From Education Research With Globally Displaced Students
text_snippet: Language Thriving: Insights From Education Research With Globally Displaced Students Language is a resource displaced people carry with them and use to manage extremely challenging circumstances. Yet research with people displaced by violence, climate change, and/or poverty tends to focus on individuals’ behavioral characteristics and deficits rather than their knowledge as they journey to new homelands. This chapter offers theory and findings of innovative intervention studies linking the discourses of diverse actors across migration systems via their relevant narratives, policies, and curricula. The projects invite participants to share experiences as global travelers interacting in problematic systems. Findings reveal young people’s creative uses of literary qualities, such as characters, plots, and evaluative devices, to navigate harsh realities of displacement and (re)settlement and, possibly, to thrive. This approach guides future research honoring human expression toward increasingly equitable and supportive educational systems.

title: Designing for These Times, Extraordinary but Not Unprecedented
text_snippet: Designing for These Times, Extraordinary but Not Unprecedented This chapter locates the current civic crises as related to long-standing histories of state violence, racialized exclusion, and dehumanization. Drawing on contemporary conditions and past scholarship, we demonstrate how border violence, moral panic, and systemic inequity shape the civic lessons students learn daily. Yet communities at the margins have continually modeled ingenuity, resistance, and futurity. Synthesizing research alongside transnational youth, organizers, and educators, we outline principles for equity-centered inquiry that blurs researcher–participant boundaries, centers storytelling, and designs toward otherwise worlds. Ultimately, this chapter contends that education research must build from community expertise to cultivate thriving, justice-oriented civic futures.

title: Educational Interbelonging: Connecting Queer and Trans Approaches to Care-Based Learning in School Systems
text_snippet: Educational Interbelonging: Connecting Queer and Trans Approaches to Care-Based Learning in School Systems This systematic review examines queer and trans (QT) studies of educational care work to join and extend transformative models of intergenerational learning in critical care ethics. By bridging QT perspectives with sociocultural learning theories, our conceptual lens expands existing ideas of pedagogy, identity, agency, and belonging to challenge and transcend paternalistic, gender-normative education reforms. Following PRISMA guidelines, we reviewed 1,244 scholarly articles from global contexts, identifying 242 that met our inclusion criteria. We found four interrelated lessons in QT literature for embedding liberatory care webs centered on “queeruptions” in school systems, with values of witnessing, intimacy, play, and imagination forming the framework’s foundation. These lessons and values contribute to our development of an ethic of “educational interbelonging,” which we offer as a conceptual map of the research and flexible, actionable model for applying transformative care resources and strategies.

title: Language and Educational Ideologies and Educational Opportunities: From “Fixing Students’ Language” to Redesigning Listening Regimes
text_snippet: Language and Educational Ideologies and Educational Opportunities: From “Fixing Students’ Language” to Redesigning Listening Regimes In the study of language and education, ideology is never merely descriptive: it names the moral and political work language does in schooling through discursive, institutional, interactional, and material arrangements that render some ways of speaking, writing, and listening legitimate while casting others as deficient or unintelligible. I argue that language ideologies become infrastructures of opportunity, organizing whose learning is legible, whose competence is audible, and whose futures remain institutionally imaginable. Framed by this RRE volume’s insistence that equity exceeds access and that thriving is a collective horizon, I map five interlocking debates—standardization/academic language; raciolinguistic listening; the “word gap”; discontinuities and gatekeeping; and multilingual schooling under monoglot and market logics—and conclude with a call for redesigning listening and assessment regimes.

title: Justice, Liberation, and Equity for Indigenous Language Well-Being and Communal Thriving
text_snippet: Justice, Liberation, and Equity for Indigenous Language Well-Being and Communal Thriving In this invited commentary, I address current tensions laid out in this special issue regarding educational systems that contribute to equity, well-being, and justice while simultaneously perpetuating unethical and harmful practices by discussing these juxtapositions in Indigenous education. I share the perspectives of several Native students and parents as they confront these tensions in their own lives with regard to Native language learning and community building. I also provide examples from the long-standing movement led by Indigenous people for Indigenous language continuity and resurgence by providing short descriptions of several initiatives to address the complexities of language revitalization faced by Indigenous people. I call for meaningful and sustained resources and policy development to support Indigenous languages in significant ways for communal well-being and thrivance.

title: Disrupting the Binaries: The Education of Latinx Peoples in the United States, Their Historical Invisibility, Collective Resilience, and New Solidarities
text_snippet: Disrupting the Binaries: The Education of Latinx Peoples in the United States, Their Historical Invisibility, Collective Resilience, and New Solidarities In this chapter, we advance a new analytic frame for understanding the educational experiences of Latinx students in the United States. This demands accounting for the historical, cultural, linguistic, racial/ethnic, geographic/spatial, and epistemological heterogeneity and intersectional specificities across Latinx communities—dimensions that are too often flattened out or ignored in research, policy, and civic life. We capture this complexity by first situating the educational experience historically for the broader Latinx community, with attention to how language policies and practices have contributed to and shaped the educational lives of students and their communities. We bring an integrated interdisciplinary perspective to further situate the historical and present educational lives of several key communities, for example, queer/trans*/gender nonbinary, Indigenous, and AfroDescendants/Afrodescendientes, who constitute Latinx communities. We build on reviews of the relevant literature to advance an analytic framework that centers on pluralities versus sustaining cultural singularity—one that moves beyond the binaries and instead focuses on who we are as heterogeneous Latinx p

title: Equitable Educational Systems That Cultivate Thriving: Expanding the Vision for Justice, Systems Transformation, and Collective Well-Being

title: Who Keeps Us Safe? We Keep Us Safe. A Commentary on the Importance of the Black Family During Dangerous Times
text_snippet: Who Keeps Us Safe? We Keep Us Safe. A Commentary on the Importance of the Black Family During Dangerous Times In this chapter, we call attention to the persistent dangers facing Black youth in the United States and the crucial role of Black families—in myriad forms—in fostering safety, resistance, and thriving. Drawing from both historical narratives and contemporary scholarship, we describe how Black families have long relied on racial socialization, or the communication and behaviors about race in our society, and community-based strategies to counter structural racism and protect youth across generations. We illustrate how these protective practices emerged during enslavement and continue today in response to ongoing inequities in education, justice, and health systems. We close with reflections on the need for collective responsibility across families, communities, and institutions to dismantle racist structures so that Black youth are not left to shoulder the burden of their own safety and survival.

title: Disciplinary Learning That Cultivates Collective Flourishing
text_snippet: Disciplinary Learning That Cultivates Collective Flourishing This chapter advances the argument that learning in the disciplines in K–12 education has the potential to support collective flourishing despite their troubled histories and role in justifying and maintaining social, political, and economic inequality. We situate this work within a decolonial project to reclaim disciplines from histories of surveillance and control by reimagining disciplinary learning as contributing to well-being, dignity, and equity. Drawing on examples from mathematics, science, and history, we argue that flourishing communities emerge when knowledge building is inclusive of marginalized peoples and honors interdependence among people, place, and planet. Central to this vision is cultivating multiple forms of agency: epistemic agency (the capacity to build and share knowledge), disciplinary agency (engaging with the constraints and possibilities of disciplinary practices), and critical agency (shaping and transforming disciplines themselves). We propose that designing learning environments to foster these agencies can position students as historical actors who use disciplinary knowledge to address everyday dilemmas, challenge inequities, and reimagine disciplin

title: Transforming Education Into a Civil Right
text_snippet: Transforming Education Into a Civil Right This commentary wrestles with the tensions between individual and collective notions of thriving in the context of civil rights and education. It begins by acknowledging that institutions of education systematically benefit some while excluding others from opportunity. We then explain the need for individual and collective rights to come together in our formulation of a civil right to education that includes both recognition of a positive right to a high-quality education that prepares students to be engaged civic participants, college and career ready, and thriving members of our society and effective protections from discrimination. The commentary concludes with pathways toward transforming education into a civil right, even amid the uphill political battle for recognizing such a right.

title: An Opportunity to Practice Living: Experimenting With a Civics of Thriving
text_snippet: An Opportunity to Practice Living: Experimenting With a Civics of Thriving In this commentary, I offer an exhortation to the field to orient research, policy, and practice in public schools toward an ethic of radical civic thriving guided by the values of interdependence, interdisciplinarity, and imagination. Rather than serving as sites where young people are trained to survive within the stratified social systems of today, schools have the potential to become intergenerational learning ecologies cultivating equitable futures. This commentary draws on scholarship in social-design-based experimentation, community-engaged partnerships, and speculative education to situate schools as sites of collective civic dreaming, offering a counternarrative to dominant discourses of individualism, scarcity, and competition.

title: Intersectionality at the Margins: A Critical Policy Analysis of Disability in Education Across Contexts
text_snippet: Intersectionality at the Margins: A Critical Policy Analysis of Disability in Education Across Contexts In this chapter, we explore how disability-related policies mediate the educational experiences of minoritized disabled students and their families, with a focus on the Global South. Expanding critical policy analysis to examine the intersections of disability with systemic oppressions, including colonialism, racism, classism, and casteism, we examine the intent and enactment of policy within specific sociopolitical, historical, and spatial contexts, investigating how policies can contribute to systems that both adversely affect and foster thriving for multiply marginalized disabled children. In our review, we found that policy design is often rooted in ahistorical, acontextual, and ableist perspectives, which limits cultural transformation and hinders collective thriving beyond compliance. We offer suggestions for creating more inclusive, transformative educational systems that better support disabled students.

title: Pursuing Equitable Education and Learning Systems: The Promise of Continuous Improvement and Design Methods
text_snippet: Pursuing Equitable Education and Learning Systems: The Promise of Continuous Improvement and Design Methods In this chapter, we wrestle with the challenge of making true progress toward building systems that cultivate collective thriving. We argue that to advance this vision, it is important to attend to change that is (a) fundamental—at the level of values, assumptions, and habits; (b) systemic—across school district central offices and ultimately all schools; and (c) equitable—variably defined as centering the knowledge, experiences, opportunities, and outcomes of historically marginalized groups. We use this conceptual framework to inform a systematic review of four specific “continuous improvement” and “design” methods that have been used across the globe as strategies for helping scholars, educators, and leaders work toward creating equitable education and learning systems. We find that each of these methods emphasizes fundamental, systemic, or equity-focused change variously defined but not all three in an integrated manner, and that use cases generally follow the methods’ priorities. By analyzing the varying affordances of these distinct methods for advancing fundamental, systemic, and equitable change in schools, our chapter offers implications for how scholars, educators, and co

title: Conceptualizing Equity and Justice in Education Policy Research: Toward a Unifying Framework and a Path Forward
text_snippet: Conceptualizing Equity and Justice in Education Policy Research: Toward a Unifying Framework and a Path Forward In this systematic review, we examine how equity and justice are conceptualized in equity-focused U.S.-based K–12 education policy scholarship published between January 2014 and June 2024. We make two key contributions: (a) We articulate a unifying framework for equity and justice, building on Nancy Fraser’s (2009) theorizing about justice and ecological conceptions of student thriving, and (b) we use this framework to evaluate the specific dimensions and characterizations of justice foregrounded in empirical studies. Ultimately, we find fragmentation in how the reviewed scholarship conceptualizes equity and justice, and we argue that transforming education systems toward collective thriving demands a robust, multidimensional, and anti-oppressive conception of justice that illuminates injustices while making space for imagining just futures. We interrogate the inherent tensions in equity-focused education policy work and highlight overlooked domains necessary for student thriving, offering a path forward for the field.
